# Introduction

Since moving to Los Angeles for graduate school, I have frequently heard people claim that "Los Angeles used to be better" because many businesses closed during the COVID-19 pandemic. Though this can most likely be said about any city throughout the world, this belief inspired me to examine how business closures changed in Los Angeles before, during, and after the pandemic. This analysis uses the "Listing of All Businesses" dataset from the Los Angeles Office of Finance, which was obtained from the City of Los Angeles Open Data Portal. This dataset contains all active and inactive registered business locations, with "active" being defined as a business whose owner has not notified the Office of Finance of a cease of operations. Relevant variables include location start and end date, council district, and the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) codes and description. This analysis measures business-location closures, as each observation represents a registered location, rather than a unique business. Simply, a business can have multiple registered locations, but if one location were to close, it would appear in this analysis.

The primary question I will try to answer with this dataset is: How did the number of business-location closures in Los Angeles change during the COVID-19 Pandemic compared with the Pre-Pandemic and Post-Pandemic periods? The COVID-19 Pandemic was defined as March 11, 2020 through May 5, 2023. The World Health Organization (WHO) declared COVID-19 a pandemic on March 11, 2020. On May 5, 2023, the WHO Director-General ended COVID-19's designation as a "...public health emergency of international concern."

References:

# Data Preparation

The "Listing of All Businesses" dataset was obtained from the City of Los Angeles Open Data Portal and is maintained by the Los Angeles Office of Finance. Because the primary question is focused on business-location closures, observations without a location end date were classified as active and excluded. Unnecessary or redundant variables, such as "mailing address" and "location description" were also removed. While combing through the dataset, I noticed that "Los Angeles" made up most of the variable "CITY," so I elected to remove it, especially since "ZIP.CODE" can be used to differentiate between parts of Los Angeles. Missing, invalid or ZIP codes outside of Los Angeles were removed. ZIP codes were restricted to their first five digits, rather than their ZIP+4 Extension. This makes it so ZIP codes represent their region rather than specific streets. ZIP codes were also restricted to a range of 90001 to 93591, as these are the ZIP codes within the boundaries of Los Angeles, according to the Los Angeles GeoHub. Dates were converted into R date objects as well. Invalid dates, those whose end dates occur before their start date, were removed. According to the data dictionary, observations whose council district is "0" are outside of the city, so these observations were removed as well as observations with missing council districts.

An initial data frame, "Closures," was created to retain historical closure records. Date-based periods were created, with "Pre-Pandemic" referring to any location end date prior to March 11, 2020. "Pandemic" refers to any location end date between March 11, 2020 and May 5, 2023. "Post-Pandemic" refers to any location end date after May 5, 2023. Future location end dates, those that have not happened yet, were removed from the "Closures" data frame. The cutoff date for this was set as October 15, 2026, the date this dataset was downloaded.

Acknowledging that the "Pre-Pandemic" category extends all the way back to 1977, a second data frame was created, "Closures_Adjusted." Here, periods were restricted to 1,151 days, which was the length of the Pandemic. "Pre-Pandemic was defined as any location end date between January 15, 2017 and March 10, 2020. "Post-Pandemic was defined as any location end date between May 6, 2023 and June 29, 2026. "Pandemic" was unchanged. Equal-length periods will make closure counts more comparable. "Closures" will be included in the Exploratory Analysis section, while "Closures_Adjusted" will be used for to answer the primary question and follow-up questions. For potential follow up questions, "Closure Month," "Closure Year," and "Closure.Month.Date" variables were created.

References

1.  https://geohub.lacity.org/datasets/lahub::zip-codes-la-county/about

```{r}
# Read in data. Create Original Data Frame. Re-format dates. 
All_Businesses <- read.csv("C:/Users/nweit/Downloads/Listing_of_All_Businesses_20261015.csv")

All_Businesses$LOCATION.START.DATE <- as.Date(All_Businesses$LOCATION.START.DATE, format = "%m/%d/%Y")
All_Businesses$LOCATION.END.DATE <- as.Date(All_Businesses$LOCATION.END.DATE, format = "%m/%d/%Y")

# Create Closures Data Frame. Remove Unnecessary Variables. Invalid Dates Removed. Removed Out-of-City Businesses. Invalid ZIP codes removed and ZIP codes reformatted. Establish Cutoff End Date. Create "Period", "Closure.Month", and "Closure.Year" Variables. 
Closures <- All_Businesses[!is.na(All_Businesses$LOCATION.END.DATE),]
Closures <- Closures[,!names(Closures) %in% c("MAILING.ZIP.CODE","DBA.NAME","LOCATION.DESCRIPTION","MAILING.CITY","MAILING.ADDRESS", "STREET.ADDRESS", "CITY")]

Closures <- Closures[is.na(Closures$LOCATION.END.DATE) | Closures$LOCATION.END.DATE >= Closures$LOCATION.START.DATE,]

Closures <- Closures[!is.na(Closures$COUNCIL.DISTRICT) & Closures$COUNCIL.DISTRICT >= 1 & Closures$COUNCIL.DISTRICT <=15,]

Clean_ZIP <- gsub("[^0-9]", "", as.character(Closures$ZIP.CODE))
Closures$ZIP.CODE <- ifelse(!is.na(Clean_ZIP) & nchar(Clean_ZIP) >=5, substr(Clean_ZIP,1,5),NA)
Closures <- Closures[!is.na(Closures$ZIP.CODE) & Closures$ZIP.CODE >= 90001 & Closures$ZIP.CODE <= 93591,]

Fixed_Date <- as.Date("2026-10-15")
Closures <- Closures[Closures$LOCATION.END.DATE <= Fixed_Date,]

Closures$Period <- ifelse(Closures$LOCATION.END.DATE < as.Date("2020-03-11"),"Pre-Pandemic", ifelse(Closures$LOCATION.END.DATE <= as.Date("2023-05-05"),"Pandemic","Post-Pandemic"))

Closures$Period <- factor(Closures$Period, levels = c("Pre-Pandemic","Pandemic","Post-Pandemic"))

Closures$Closure.Month <- format(Closures$LOCATION.END.DATE, format = "%m")
Closures$Closure.Year <- format(Closures$LOCATION.END.DATE, format = "%Y")
Closures$Closure.Month.Date <- as.Date(format(Closures$LOCATION.END.DATE, "%Y-%m-01"))


# Create Closures_Adjusted with January 15, 2017 and June 29,2026 as the Cutoff End Dates.
Closures_Adjusted <- Closures[Closures$LOCATION.END.DATE >= as.Date("2017-01-15") & Closures$LOCATION.END.DATE <= as.Date("2026-06-29"),]
```

# Exploratory Analysis

For the Exploratory Analysis, I will be using both the "Closures" and "Closures_Adjusted" data frames. "Closures" includes all records from November 14, 1977 and October 15, 2026. "Closures_Adjusted" includes all records from January 15, 2017 and June 29, 2026. For each visualization, "Historic Data" will refer to the "Closures" data frame and "Adjusted Data" will refer to the "Closures_Adjusted" data frame.

```{r}
knitr::kable(Table, col.names = c("Dataset Characteristic", "Value"), caption = "Business Closure Characteristics (Adjusted Data)")

```

### Explanation

The Historic Data table reveals that there were a total of 648,311 closures between November 14, 1977 and October 14, 2026, which was the latest closure at the time this data was downloaded. Given that each business location gets a unique location account, it makes sense that the number of unique location accounts matches the number of business-location closures. Of the closures, 590,629 had unique business names, suggesting that some business names were associated with multiple locations. However, variation in business names was not accounted for, so business names alone cannot determine the exact number of unique businesses. Approximately 99% of the NAICS codes, industry descriptions, and locations were missing. While this won't affect the primary analysis, this may limit follow-up question analyses.

The Adjusted Data table reveals that there were a total of 234,605 closures between January 15, 2017 and June 29, 2026. Again, given that each business location gets a unique location account, it makes sense that the number of unique location accounts matches the number of business-location closures. There were 220,944 unique business names, but again, variation in business names were not accounted for, so this value should not be interpreted as the exact number of unique business. 98.7% of the NAICS codes, industry descriptions, and locations were missing. Again, this may limit follow-up question analyses.

## Annual Business-Location Closures (Historic and Adjusted Data)

```{r}
# Closures by Year (Historic Data)
Yearly_Closures <- as.data.frame(table(Closures$Closure.Year))
names(Yearly_Closures) <- c("Year", "Closures")
Yearly_Closures$Year <- as.integer(as.character(Yearly_Closures$Year))

Year_Count <- table(Closures$Closure.Year)
All_Years <- seq(min(Closures$Closure.Year, na.rm = TRUE), max(Closures$Closure.Year, na.rm = TRUE))
Yearly_Closures <- data.frame(Year = All_Years, Closures = as.numeric(Year_Count[as.character(All_Years)]))

par(mar = c(7,5,4,2) + 0.1)
barplot(Yearly_Closures$Closures, names.arg = Yearly_Closures$Year, las = 2, border = NA, cex.names = 0.6, col = "blue", xlab = "Closure Year", ylab = "Number of Closures", main = "Annual Business-Location Closures (Historic Data)", sub = "Note: 1977 and 2026 are Incomplete Years.")

# Closures by Year (Adjusted Data)
Yearly_Closures <- as.data.frame(table(Closures_Adjusted$Closure.Year))
names(Yearly_Closures) <- c("Year", "Closures")
Yearly_Closures$Year <- as.integer(as.character(Yearly_Closures$Year))

Year_Count <- table(Closures_Adjusted$Closure.Year)
All_Years <- seq(min(Closures_Adjusted$Closure.Year, na.rm = TRUE), max(Closures_Adjusted$Closure.Year, na.rm = TRUE))
Yearly_Closures <- data.frame(Year = All_Years, Closures = as.numeric(Year_Count[as.character(All_Years)]))

barplot(Yearly_Closures$Closures, names.arg = Yearly_Closures$Year, las = 2, col = "blue", xlab = "Closure Year", ylab = "Number of Closures", main = "Annual Business-Location Closures (Adjusted Data)", sub = "Note: 2017 and 2026 are Incomplete Years.")
```

### Explanation

The annual distribution of the Historic Data indicates that closure data before the 2000's are relatively sparse, though, this could be because of limited reporting or data availability. Prominent peaks in closures occurred in 2004, 2013, and 2017, which may warrant further investigation to determine if they represent drastic changes in closures, reporting patterns, or some other reason. As stated on the barplot, 1977 and 2026 are incomplete years. the 1977 records begin on November 14, 1977 and the 2026 records end on October 14, 2026. Their closures should not be directly compared to the closures of complete years.

The annual distribution of the Adjusted Data covers the equal length, 1,151-day Pre-Pandemic, Pandemic, and Post-Pandemic periods. This barplot does not show separate study periods, rather, it shows complete calendar-year closure totals. This means that there is some overlap between the periods in 2020 (Pre-Pandemic and Pandemic) and 2023 (Pandemic and Post-Pandemic). The prominent peak in 2017 is still present in this data. As stated, 2017 and 2026 are incomplete years. 2017 begins on January 15, 2017 and 2026 ends on June 29, 2026. Their closures should not be directly compared to the closures of complete years.

## Monthly Business-Location Closures (Historic and Adjusted Data)

```{r}
# Closures by Month (Historic Data)
Monthly_Closures <- aggregate(rep(1,nrow(Closures)), by = list(Closure_Month = Closures$Closure.Month.Date), FUN = sum)
names(Monthly_Closures)[2] <- "Closures"

plot(Monthly_Closures$Closure_Month, Monthly_Closures$Closures, type = "l", col = "blue", xaxt = "n", xlab = "Closure Month", ylab = "Number of Closures", main = "Monthly Business-Location Closures (Historic Data)")
Axis_Dates <- seq(from = min(Monthly_Closures$Closure_Month), to = max(Monthly_Closures$Closure_Month), by = "3 months")
axis.Date(side = 1, at = Axis_Dates, format = "%b %Y", cex.axis = 0.8)

abline(v = as.Date("2020-03-11"), col = "red", lty = 2)
abline(v = as.Date("2023-05-05"),col = "red")
legend("topleft", legend = c("Monthly Closures", "Pandemic Begins", "Pandemic Ends"), col = c("blue", "red", "red"), lty = c(1,2,1), lwd = 1)

Largest_Month <- Monthly_Closures[Monthly_Closures$Closures == max(Monthly_Closures$Closures, na.rm = TRUE),,drop = FALSE]
Largest_Month$Month <- format(Largest_Month$Closure_Month,"%B %Y")
Largest_Month <- Largest_Month[, c("Month", "Closures")]
knitr::kable(Largest_Month, col.names = c("Closure Month", "Number of Closures"), format.args = list(big.mark = ","),caption = paste("Month with the Largest Number of Business-Location Closures (Historic Data"), row.names = FALSE)

# Closures by Month (Adjusted Data)
Monthly_Closures <- aggregate(rep(1,nrow(Closures_Adjusted)), by = list(Closure_Month = Closures_Adjusted$Closure.Month.Date), FUN = sum)
names(Monthly_Closures)[2] <- "Closures"

plot(Monthly_Closures$Closure_Month, Monthly_Closures$Closures, type = "l", col = "blue", xaxt = "n", xlab = "Closure Month", ylab = "Number of Closures", main = "Monthly Business-Location Closures (Adjusted Data)")
Axis_Dates <- seq(from = min(Monthly_Closures$Closure_Month), to = max(Monthly_Closures$Closure_Month), by = "3 months")
axis.Date(side = 1, at = Axis_Dates, format = "%b %Y", cex.axis = 0.8)

abline(v = as.Date("2020-03-11"), col = "red", lty = 2)
abline(v = as.Date("2023-05-05"),col = "red")
legend("topright", legend = c("Monthly Closures", "Pandemic Begins", "Pandemic Ends"), col = c("blue", "red", "red"), lty = c(1,2,1), lwd = 1)

Largest_Month <- Monthly_Closures[Monthly_Closures$Closures == max(Monthly_Closures$Closures, na.rm = TRUE),,drop = FALSE]
Largest_Month$Month <- format(Largest_Month$Closure_Month,"%B %Y")
Largest_Month <- Largest_Month[, c("Month", "Closures")]
knitr::kable(Largest_Month, col.names = c("Closure Month", "Number of Closures"), format.args = list(big.mark = ","),caption = paste("Month with the Largest Number of Business-Location Closures (Adjusted Data"), row.names = FALSE)
```

### Explanation

The monthly distribution of the Historic Data shows greater variation in closures over time than the annual distribution. Like the annual distribution, data before the 2000's is relatively sparse. The monthly distribution reveals more pronounced peaks, which may suggest that the peaks in the annual distribution come from a large amount of closures in certain months rather than high amounts of closures throughout the entire year. The highest monthly peak in closures occurs in November 2004, with 41,575 closures.

The monthly distribution of the Adjusted Data provides a more detailed view of closures across the three periods. Prominent peaks occur in the Pre-Pandemic period. Monthly closures appear lower during the Pandemic, and remain relatively low during the Post-Pandemic period except for one peak at sometime in 2024. The highest monthly peak in closures occurs in March 2017, with 14,993 closures.

## Closures by Period (Historic Data)

```{r}
# Closures by Period (Historic Data)
Period_Count <- as.data.frame(table(Closures$Period))
names(Period_Count) <- c("Period","Closures")
Period_Count$Percentage <- round(100*Period_Count$Closures / sum(Period_Count$Closures),2)
knitr::kable(Period_Count, format.args = list(big.mark = ","), col.names = c("Period", "Closures", "Percentage"), caption = "Business-Location Closures by Period (Historic Data)")
```

### Explanation

While the Adjusted Data table will be a part of the Preliminary Results section, I included the Historic Data here to describe the data. The table summarizes the distribution of business-location closures across the periods in the Historic Data. Of the 648,311 closures, 511,189 (78.85%) occurred during the Pre-Pandemic period. 66,954 (10.33%) occurred during the Pandemic, and 70,168 (10.82%) occurred during the Post-Pandemic period. These percentages should only be treated as a description of the data rather than a direct comparison among periods, as the periods cover unequal lengths of time. This is especially true for the Pre-Pandemic period, which covers November 14, 1977 to March 10, 2020. Therefore, the large percentage of Pre-Pandemic closures reflects its large observation period.

# Preliminary Results

I will not include the Historic Data in this section because the Pre-Pandemic period contains more than 42 years-worth of data. Comparing closure counts across these unequal periods would be misleading. Instead, I will use the Adjusted Data throughout this section because it is divided into equal-length, 1,151-day periods. These equal periods provide an appropriate basis for answering the primary and follow-up questions.

## Primary Question

How did the number of business-location closures in Los Angeles change during the COVID-19 Pandemic compared with the Pre-Pandemic and Post-Pandemic periods?

```{r}
# Business-Location Closures across Periods
Counts <- table(Closures_Adjusted$Period)
Results <- data.frame(Period = c("Pre-Pandemic", "Pandemic", "Post-Pandemic"),Start_Date = as.Date(c("2017-01-15","2020-03-11","2023-05-06")), End_Date = as.Date(c("2020-03-10", "2023-05-05", "2026-06-29")), Days = c(1151, 1151, 1151), Closures = as.numeric(Counts[c("Pre-Pandemic", "Pandemic", "Post-Pandemic")]))

Results$Mean_Daily_Closures <- Results$Closures / Results$Days
Results$Percentage <- 100 * c(Results$Closures / sum(Results$Closures))

knitr::kable(Results, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE, col.names = c("Period","Start Date", "End Date", "Days", "Closures", "Mean Daily Closures", "Percentage of Closures"), format.args = list(big.mark =","), caption = paste("Business-Location Closures across Periods"))

# Change in Business-Location Closures across Periods
Pandemic_vs_Pre_Difference <- Counts["Pandemic"] - Counts["Pre-Pandemic"]
Pandemic_vs_Pre_Percent <- 100 * (Counts["Pandemic"] / Counts["Pre-Pandemic"] - 1)
Post_vs_Pandemic_Difference <-Counts["Post-Pandemic"] - Counts["Pandemic"]
Post_vs_Pandemic_Percent <- 100 * (Counts["Post-Pandemic"] / Counts["Pandemic"] - 1)

Comparison_Table <- data.frame(Comparison = c("Pre-Pandemic vs. Pandemic", "Pandemic vs. Post-Pandemic"), Earlier_Closures = c(unname(Counts["Pre-Pandemic"]), unname(Counts["Pandemic"])), Later_Closures = c(unname(Counts["Pandemic"]), unname(Counts["Post-Pandemic"])), Difference = c(unname(Pandemic_vs_Pre_Difference), unname(Post_vs_Pandemic_Difference)), Percent_Change = c(unname(Pandemic_vs_Pre_Percent), unname(Post_vs_Pandemic_Percent)))
knitr::kable(Comparison_Table, digits = 2, format.args = list(big.mark = ","), col.names = c("Comparison", "Earlier Period Closures", "Later Period Closures", "Difference", "Percent Change"), caption = paste("Change in Business-Location Closures across Periods"))

Period_Colors <- c("blue","red","green")
Bar_Labels <- paste0(format(Results$Closures, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE), "\n(",sprintf("%.2f", Results$Percentage), "%)")
Bar_Positions <- barplot(Results$Closures, names.arg = Results$Period, col = Period_Colors, ylim = c(0, max(Results$Closures) * 1.20), xlab = "Period", ylab = "Number of Closures", main = "Business-Location Closures across Periods")
text(x = Bar_Positions, y = Results$Closures, labels = Bar_Labels, pos = 3)


```

### Summary

To answer the primary question, I used the Adjusted Data table, as it includes three equal length periods of 1,151 days, allowing their business-location closure counts to be compared directly. The Pre-Pandemic period had 100,854 closures, representing 42.99% of all closures. The Pandemic had 66,954 closures (28.54%) and the Post-Pandemic period had 66.797 closures (28.47%). The number of business-location closures decreased by 33,900, or 33.61%, from the Pre-Pandemic period to the Pandemic period. Mean daily closures had a similar decrease across these periods, going from 87.62 to 58.17. The number of business-location closures decreased by only 157, or 0.23%, from the Pandemic to the Post-Pandemic period. Mean daily closures barely decreased from 58.17 to 58.03. Therefore, business-location closures declined substantially during the Pandemic and remained relatively unchanged afterward. The accompanying barplot visually summarizes these results.

## Follow-Up Question 1

Which industries experienced the greatest changes in closure frequency during the Pandemic?

Here, I will use the Adjusted Data again, however, I will remove any businesses missing the NAICS codes and industry descriptions. As revealed in the Exploratory Analysis, 98.7% of observations in the data frame are missing from these variables. Taking this into account, a revised version of the question would be: Among business locations with available NAICS codes and industry descriptions, which industries experienced the largest changes in closures during the Pandemic compared with the Pre-Pandemic and Post-Pandemic periods?

```{r}
Industry_Closures <- Closures_Adjusted[!is.na(Closures_Adjusted$NAICS) & trimws(as.character(Closures_Adjusted$NAICS)) !="" & !is.na(Closures_Adjusted$PRIMARY.NAICS.DESCRIPTION) & trimws(as.character(Closures_Adjusted$PRIMARY.NAICS.DESCRIPTION)) != "",]

Industry_Counts <- as.data.frame.matrix(xtabs(~ PRIMARY.NAICS.DESCRIPTION + Period, data = Industry_Closures))
Industry_Counts$Industry <- rownames(Industry_Counts)
rownames(Industry_Counts) <- NULL

# Pre- vs Pandemic Table
Industry_Counts$Pre_vs_Pandemic_Difference <- Industry_Counts$Pandemic - Industry_Counts$`Pre-Pandemic`

Industry_Counts$Pre_vs_Pandemic_Percent <- ifelse(Industry_Counts$`Pre-Pandemic` > 0, 100 * ( Industry_Counts$Pandemic / Industry_Counts$`Pre-Pandemic` - 1), NA)

Largest_Pre_vs_Pandemic <- Industry_Counts[order(abs(Industry_Counts$Pre_vs_Pandemic_Difference), decreasing = TRUE),]
Largest_Pre_vs_Pandemic <- head(Largest_Pre_vs_Pandemic,10)
Largest_Pre_vs_Pandemic <- Largest_Pre_vs_Pandemic[, c("Industry","Pre-Pandemic","Pandemic","Pre_vs_Pandemic_Difference","Pre_vs_Pandemic_Percent")]

knitr::kable(Largest_Pre_vs_Pandemic, digits = 2, col.names = c("Industry", "Pre-Pandemic Closures", "Pandemic Closures", "Difference","Percent Change"), format.args = list(big.mark = ","), caption = paste("Industries with the Largest Changes in Closures from Pre-Pandemic to Pandemic"), row.names = FALSE)

# Pandemic vs Post- Table
Industry_Counts$Pandemic_vs_Post_Difference <- Industry_Counts$`Post-Pandemic` - Industry_Counts$Pandemic

Industry_Counts$Pandemic_vs_Post_Percent <- ifelse(Industry_Counts$Pandemic > 0, 100 * ( Industry_Counts$`Post-Pandemic` / Industry_Counts$Pandemic - 1), NA)

Largest_Pandemic_vs_Post <- Industry_Counts[order(abs(Industry_Counts$Pandemic_vs_Post_Difference), decreasing = TRUE),]
Largest_Pandemic_vs_Post <- head(Largest_Pandemic_vs_Post,10)
Largest_Pandemic_vs_Post <- Largest_Pandemic_vs_Post[, c("Industry","Pandemic","Post-Pandemic","Pandemic_vs_Post_Difference","Pandemic_vs_Post_Percent")]

knitr::kable(Largest_Pandemic_vs_Post, digits = 2, col.names = c("Industry", "Pandemic Closures", "Post-Pandemic Closures","Difference","Percent Change"), format.args = list(big.mark = ","), caption = paste("Industries with the Largest Changes in Closures from Pandemic to Post-Pandemic"), row.names = FALSE)
```

### Summary

The first table displays the top ten industries with the largest absolute changes in closures between the Pre-Pandemic period and Pandemic. The second table displays the top ten industries with the largest absolute changes between the Pandemic and Post-Pandemic period. percentage changes are included to show the size of each change relative to the earlier period. The results were ranked according to the absolute difference in closure counts.

Among business location with available NAICS codes and industry descriptions, "All other personal services" experienced the largest decrease in closures from the Pre-Pandemic period to the Pandemic, declining from 63 to 31, a decrease of 50.79%. This same industry also had the largest increase in closures from the Pandemic to the Post-Pandemic period, rising from 31 to 71, an increase of 129.03%. All ten of the largest absolute changes between the Pre-Pandemic period and Pandemic were decreases. Conversely, all ten of the largest absolute changes between the Pandemic and Post-Pandemic period were increases.

This analysis included only those records with non-missing NAICS codes and industry descriptions. Of the 234,605 records in the Adjusted Data, approximately 98.7% were excluded, leaving only 2,943 records for this analysis. Therefore, these tables provide a samll description of the industry closure patterns and may not represent full industry closures patterns across Los Angeles.

## Follow-Up Question 2

How were business-location closures spatially distributed across Los Angeles over all three periods? How were business-location closures spatially distributed across Los Angeles for each period?

```{r district-map, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(sf)

Map_Data <- Closures_Adjusted[!is.na(Closures_Adjusted$LOCATION) & trimws(as.character(Closures_Adjusted$LOCATION)) != "", ]

Clean_Locations <- gsub("[()]", "", trimws(as.character(Map_Data$LOCATION)))
Coordinates <- do.call(rbind, strsplit(Clean_Locations, ","))
Map_Data$Latitude <- as.numeric(trimws(Coordinates[,1]))
Map_Data$Longitude <- as.numeric(trimws(Coordinates[,2]))

Map_Points <- st_as_sf(Map_Data, coords = c("Longitude","Latitude"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE)

Council_Districts <- st_read(paste0("https://data.lacity.org/api/geospatial/pxeu-7j74?method=export&format=GeoJSON"), quiet = TRUE)
Council_Districts <- st_transform(Council_Districts, crs = 4326)

Council_Districts$District_Label <- as.integer(as.character(Council_Districts$name))
District_Labels <- st_transform(Council_Districts, crs = 3857)
District_Labels <- st_point_on_surface(District_Labels)
District_Labels <- st_transform(District_Labels, crs = 4326)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = Council_Districts, fill = "gray", color = "black") + 
  geom_sf(data = Map_Points, color = "blue", size = 0.5, alpha = 0.3) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-118.70, -118.15), ylim = c(33.70, 34.35), expand = FALSE) + 
  geom_sf_text(data = District_Labels, aes(label = District_Label), color = "white", size = 5, fontface = "bold", check_overlap = TRUE) + 
  labs(title = paste("Business-Location Closures by Council District"), x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude")
```

```{r district-map, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}

ggplot() +

ggplot() +

ggplot() +

```

### Summary

The combined map displays business-location closures by council district across all three periods. In other words, it is a map that combines all closures over time, rather than separating into each period. Approximately 98.7% of location values were missing, so this map only displays business-location closures with valid locations across all three periods. Compared to the official Council District map (https://culture.lacity.gov/council-districts-directory), closures appear concentrated in Council Districts 1, 10, 13, and 14 which is the area with the dense amount of points. Council District 1 includes parts of Lincoln Heights, Koreatown, Cypress Park, and University Park. Council District 10 includes parts of Arlington Heights, Koreatown, Olympic Park, and West Pico. Council District 13 includes parts of Silver lake, Echo Park, Hollywood, East Hollywood, and Koreatown. Council District 14 includes parts of Downtown Los Angeles, Boyle Heights, Eagle Rock, Lincoln Heights, and Monterey Hills.

The period-specific maps provide a clearer view of the spatial distribution of closures over time. During the Pre-Pandemic period, closures appear concentrated in Council Districts 1, 10, 13, and 14. The Pandemic map shows that closures concentrated in Council Districts 10 and 14. The Post-Pandemic period map shows that closures concentrated in Council Districts 1, 10, 11, 13, and 14. Council District 11 includes Bentwood, Del Rey, Mar Vista, Pacific Palisades, and Venice.

### Summary

The tables rank all Council Districts according to the absolute change in business-location closures between consecutive periods. From the Pre-Pandemic period to the Pandemic, Council District 14 experienced the largest absolute change. Its closures decreased from 9,713 to 6,429, a decrease in 3,284 closures (a 33.81% decrease). Every other Council District also recorded fewer closures during the Pandemic period. Council District 14 includes parts of Downtown Los Angeles, Boyle Heights, Eagle Rock, Lincoln Heights, and Monterey Hills. From the Pandemic to the Post-Pandemic period, Council District 5 experienced the largest absolute change. Its closures decreased from 7,744 to 6,813, a decrease in 931 closures (a 12.02% decrease). This district includes Bel-Air, Beverlywood, Century City, and Carthay Circle. Some districts did experience an increase in closures in the Post-Pandemic period, with the largest increase occuring in Council District 9. Here, closures increased from 1,974 to 2,330, an increase of 356 closures (a 18.03% increase). This district includes some of Downtown Los Angeles, University Park, Exposition Park, South Central, and South Park.

The accompanying maps display the changes geographically. Red represents a decrease in closures while blue represents an increase in closures. The darker the color, the greater the magnitude of change. The Pre-Pandemic vs. Pandemic map periods shows that all districts experienced decreases in closures, and that Council District 14 had the largest decrease between the two periods. The Pandemic vs. Post-Pandemic map shows that Council District 5 had the largest decrease in closures and that Council District 9 had the largest increase in closures between the two periods.

## Follow-Up Question 5

Was the percentage of businesses-location closures that operated for one year or less ("recently established") higher during the Pandemic than the Pre- and Post-Pandemic periods?

```{r}
Duration <- Closures_Adjusted[!is.na(Closures_Adjusted$LOCATION.START.DATE),]
Duration$Duration_Days <- as.numeric(Duration$LOCATION.END.DATE - Duration$LOCATION.START.DATE)
Duration$Recently_Established <- Duration$Duration_Days <= 365

Total_by_Period <- as.data.frame(table(Duration$Period))
names(Total_by_Period) <- c("Period", "Closures_with_Start_Date")

Recent_By_Period <- aggregate(as.integer(Recently_Established) ~ Period, data = Duration, FUN = sum)

names(Recent_By_Period)[2] <- "Recently_Established_Closures"

Recent_Summary <- merge(Total_by_Period, Recent_By_Period, by = "Period")
Recent_Summary$Percent_Recently_Established <- 100 * (Recent_Summary$Recently_Established_Closures / Recent_Summary$Closures_with_Start_Date)
Recent_Summary$Period <- factor(Recent_Summary$Period, levels = c("Pre-Pandemic","Pandemic","Post-Pandemic"))
Recent_Summary <- Recent_Summary[order(Recent_Summary$Period),]

knitr::kable(Recent_Summary, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE, col.names = c("Period", "Total Closures", "Closed within One Year", "Percentage"), format.args = list(big.mark = ","), caption = paste("Recently Established Buisness-Location Closures by Period"))

barplot(Recent_Summary$Percent_Recently_Established, names.arg = Recent_Summary$Period, col = c("blue", "red", "green"), xlab = "Period", ylab = "Percent of Closures", main = paste("Recently Established Busienss-Location Closures by Period"), ylim =c(0,6))
```

### Summary

Recently established business-locations accounted for 5.88% of Pre-Pandemic period closures, 4.04% of Pandemic closures, and 2.27% of Post-Pandemic period closures. Therefore, the percentage of recently established business-location closures was not higher during the Pandemic compared to the Pre-Pandemic period, but was higher during the Pandemic compared to the Post-Pandemic period. Overall, recently established business-location closures declined during the Pandemic and continued to decline in the Post-Pandemic period. These findings do not show that recently established businesses had a lower risk of closing, as businesses that remained open were not included, so the closure rate of all recently established businesses could not be calculated.

## Follow-Up Question 6

Which complete calendar months had the largest numbers of reported business-location closures within each period?

For this question, the partial months of January 2017, March 2020,, May 2023, and June 2026 were excluded, as they do not contain a complete month of observations within their assigned periods.

```{r}
Complete_Months <- Closures_Adjusted[!Closures_Adjusted$Closure.Month.Date %in% as.Date(c("2017-01-01","2020-03-01","2023-05-01","2026-06-01")),]

Monthly_Closures <- aggregate(rep(1, nrow(Complete_Months)), by = list(Closure_Month = Complete_Months$Closure.Month.Date, Period = Complete_Months$Period), FUN = sum)
names(Monthly_Closures)[3] <- "Closures"

Monthly_Closures$Period_Maximum <- ave(Monthly_Closures$Closures, Monthly_Closures$Period, FUN = max)
Largest_Month <- Monthly_Closures[Monthly_Closures$Closures == Monthly_Closures$Period_Maximum,]
Largest_Month$Month <- format(Largest_Month$Closure_Month,"%B %Y")
Largest_Month$Period <- factor(Largest_Month$Period, levels = c("Pre-Pandemic", "Pandemic", "Post-Pandemic"))
Largest_Month <- Largest_Month[order(Largest_Month$Period), c("Period", "Month", "Closures")]

knitr::kable(Largest_Month, col.names = c("Period", "Closure Month", "Number of Closures"), row.names = FALSE, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),caption = paste("Months with the Largest Number of Business-Location Closures"))
```

### Summary

The largest monthly business-location closures during the Pre-Pandemic period occurred in March 2017, with 14,993 closures. The largest monthly business-location closures during the Pandemic occurred in December 2020, with 5,821 closures. Lastly, the largest monthly business-location closures during the Post-Pandemic period occurred in October 2024, with 8,626 closures. Among the three periods, the Pre-Pandemic had the highest peak monthly closures and the Pandemic had the lowest peak monthly closures. The data alone cannot determine the reason for each peak, as it could be the result of actual increases in closure patterns, an increase in data availability, a change in reporting procedures, or some other reason. 

## Follow-Up Question 7

How did the variability of monthly closure counts differ across the three periods?

For this question, the partial months of January 2017, March 2020,, May 2023, and June 2026 were removed, as they do not contain a complete month of observations within their assigned periods. Including these months could possibly lower monthly closure counts and distort variability measures. 

```{r period-summary, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
Monthly_Mean <- aggregate(Closures ~ Period, data = Monthly_Closures, FUN = mean)

Monthly_Median <- aggregate(Closures ~ Period, data = Monthly_Closures, FUN = median)

Monthly_SD <- aggregate(Closures ~ Period, data = Monthly_Closures, FUN = sd)

Monthly_Min <- aggregate(Closures ~ Period, data = Monthly_Closures, FUN = min)

Monthly_Max <- aggregate(Closures ~ Period,data = Monthly_Closures,FUN = max)

Monthly_IQR <- aggregate(Closures ~ Period, data = Monthly_Closures, FUN = IQR)

Monthly_CV <- aggregate(Closures ~ Period, data = Monthly_Closures, FUN = function(x) 100 * sd(x)/mean(x))


Period_Summary <- Reduce(function(x, y) merge(x, y, by = "Period"),list(Monthly_Mean, Monthly_Median, Monthly_SD, Monthly_Min, Monthly_Max, Monthly_IQR, Monthly_CV))
names(Period_Summary) <- c("Period", "Mean", "Median", "SD", "Minimum", "Maximum", "IQR", "CV")
Period_Summary$Period <- factor(Period_Summary$Period,levels = c("Pre-Pandemic", "Pandemic", "Post-Pandemic"))
Period_Summary <- Period_Summary[order(Period_Summary$Period),]
Period_Summary <- Period_Summary[,c("Period", "Mean", "Median",  "Minimum", "Maximum", "SD", "IQR", "CV")]

knitr::kable(Period_Summary, digits = 2, format.args = list(big.mark = ","), row.names = FALSE, col.names = c("Period", "Mean", "Median", "Minimum", "Maximum", "Standard Deviation", "IQR", "CV"),caption = "Monthly Business-Location Closures by Period")

boxplot(Closures ~ Period, data = Monthly_Closures, col = c("blue", "red", "green"), border = "gray", xlab = "Period", ylab = "Monthly Closures", main = "Distribution of Monthly Closures by Period")
```

### Summary

Monthly closure counts had the greatest variability during the Pre-Pandemic period, with a standard deviation of 3,212.88 and a coefficient of variation of 119.20%. The Post-Pandemic period had the second-highest variability, with a standard deviation of 1,643.65 and a coefficient of variation of 91.62%. The Pandemic had the lowest variability, with a standard deviation of 1,144.87 and a coefficient of variation of 64.71%. However, the Pandemic had the largest interquartile range at 689.0 closures, compared to 634.0 in the Pre-Pandemic period and 463.5 in the Post-Pandemic period. This implies that the middle 50% of monthly closure counts were the most dispersed during the Pandemic. The boxplot suggests that the larger standard deviations and coefficients of variations of the Pre- and Post-Pandemic periods stem from outlier months, or months with unusually high closure counts. So, the Pre-Pandemic period had the greatest overall variability, but the Pandemic had the greatest variability among the middle 50% of monthly records.

# Conclusion

This analysis examined how reported business-location closures in Los Angeles changed across equal-length Pre-Pandemic, Pandemic, and Post-Pandemic periods. Total closures decreased from 100,854 during the Pre-Pandemic period to 66,954 during the Pandemic and to 66,797 during the Post-Pandemic period. Therefore, reported closures declined substantially during the Pandemic compared with the Pre-Pandemic period and remained relatively unchanged afterward.

Additional analyses revealed variation across industries and geographic areas. Of records with valid industry information, "All other personal services" had the largest decrease in closures from the Pre-Pandemic period to the Pandemic and the largest increase from the Pandemic to the Post-Pandemic period. According to the NAICS website, this category includes services like bail bonding and personal training, among many others. From the Pre-Pandemic period to the Pandemic, Council District 14 experienced the largest decline in closures. From the Pandemic to the Post-Pandemic period, Council District 5 had the largest decline in closures and Council District 9 had the largest increase. ZIP code 91331 experienced the largest decrease in closures during the Pandemic, while ZIP code 90014 experienced the largest increase in closures after the Pandemic. ZIP code 90049 had the largest decrease in the closures after the Pandemic as well. These ZIP codes are within Council Districts 6 and 7, 14, and 11, respectively. The percentage of closures of recently established businesses, those that operated for one year or less, was calculated using valid records. The percentage of recently established business-location closures across all three periods declined. Monthly closure counts were the most variable during the Pre-Pandemic period, though, the middle 50% of monthly closure counts were the most dispersed during the Pandemic. 

These findings describe the changes in reported closures, but do not show that the Pandemic caused them. Missing information in the original dataset, possible changes in reporting procedures, and the exclusion of active businesses limit the conclusions that can be made. Nonetheless, the analysis shows that the number of reported business-location closures was lower during and after the Pandemic than during the Pre-Pandemic period. Along with that, closure patterns varied across industries, time, and geographic areas.
